## Background

@holland1990dutch introduced the **Dutch Identity** — an exact result about
the joint distribution of dichotomous item responses under a unidimensional IRT
model. It says that the *manifest* (unconditional) probability of a response
pattern $\mathbf{x} = (x_1, \ldots, x_J) \in \{0,1\}^J$ can be written as an
exponential family whose sufficient statistics are functions of the item
responses. Holland then conjectured that, for long tests with smooth item
response functions (IRFs), this is well approximated by something strikingly
simple:

$$\log p(\mathbf{x}) \approx \alpha + \sum_{j=1}^{J} \beta_j x_j + \frac{1}{2}\!\left(\sum_{j=1}^{J} \gamma_j x_j\right)^{\!2}$$

This is log-quadratic in the $x_j$, requires only $2J + 1$ parameters regardless
of $J$, and makes precise predictions about the structure of second-order
interactions between items. Note that the identity and the approximation are
different things. The identity holds exactly; the approximation is a conjecture,
and @zhang1997holland give unidimensional models for which it fails, so it does
not follow from smoothness and unidimensionality alone, nor is it guaranteed to
improve as $J$ grows. What follows treats the log-quadratic form as a model to
be checked against data rather than as a consequence of IRT, and the results are
evidence about these datasets. Holland's paper also contains a corollary about
total-score distributions under the Rasch model and a proposed conservation law
for the number of parameters a long test supports; neither is taken up here.

::: {.callout-note}
All figures use pre-computed results; the scripts behind each are listed under
Reproducibility. The single table used throughout Sections 1–2 is **`r s1_3$table_name`**
($J = `r s1_3$J`$ items, $N = `r format(s1_3$N, big.mark=",")`$ respondents,
computed `r format(date_run, "%B %Y")`).
:::

---

## Section 1: The manifest probabilities directly

```{r}
#| label: s1-concentration
#| echo: false
#| eval: true

# Concentration of p(x) under the observed frequencies and the two fitted
# models, from the cached pattern table. The corpus-wide version of these
# numbers is vignettes/dutch_identity_gapshare.R with CONCENTRATION=1.
s1c <- if (!is.null(s1_3$patterns)) {
  pt <- s1_3$patterns
  X  <- as.matrix(pt[, s1_3$item_cols])
  pr <- list(obs = pt$count / sum(pt$count), ind = exp(pt$log_p_ind), rq = exp(pt$log_p_rq))
  pr <- lapply(pr, function(p) p / sum(p))
  H  <- vapply(pr, function(p) { p <- p[p > 0]; -sum(p * log2(p)) }, numeric(1))
  all1 <- rowSums(X) == ncol(X)
  list(
    n_cells   = nrow(pt), n_obs = sum(pt$count > 0), min_count = min(pt$count),
    top1      = vapply(pr, max, numeric(1)),
    top5      = vapply(pr, function(p) sum(sort(p, decreasing = TRUE)[1:min(5, length(p))]), numeric(1)),
    top_is_all0 = vapply(pr, function(p) all(X[which.max(p), ] == 0), logical(1)),
    H = H, eff = 2^H,
    multi    = H[["ind"]] - H[["obs"]],
    rq_share = (H[["ind"]] - H[["rq"]]) / (H[["ind"]] - H[["obs"]]),
    all1_ratio = pr$obs[all1] / pr$ind[all1]
  )
} else list(n_cells = NA, n_obs = NA, min_count = NA,
            top1 = c(obs = NA, ind = NA, rq = NA), top5 = c(obs = NA, ind = NA, rq = NA),
            top_is_all0 = c(obs = NA, ind = NA, rq = NA),
            H = c(obs = NA, ind = NA, rq = NA), eff = c(obs = NA, ind = NA, rq = NA),
            multi = NA, rq_share = NA, all1_ratio = NA)
pct <- function(x) paste0(round(100 * x, 1), "%")
s1c$caption <- paste0(
  "Empirical manifest probabilities of all 2^J response patterns, ranked from most to ",
  "least common (log scale). ",
  if (isTRUE(s1c$n_obs == s1c$n_cells))
    paste0("Every pattern is observed at least once (the rarest ", s1c$min_count,
           " times), so no point is grey. ")
  else "Patterns never observed are grey. ",
  "The most common pattern holds ", pct(s1c$top1[["obs"]]), " of respondents and the five ",
  "most common hold ", pct(s1c$top5[["obs"]]), ". Hover over a point to see its response pattern.")
```

For a test of $J$ binary items, a respondent's answers define a response pattern
$\mathbf{x} \in \{0,1\}^J$. There are $2^J$ possible patterns, each occurring
with manifest probability $p(\mathbf{x})$. Before modeling, it is worth asking:
what do these probabilities actually look like? @holland1990dutch motivates the
loglinear approach because, for large $J$, the $p(\mathbf{x})$ are too numerous
and too sparse to estimate one cell at a time. This table is not in that regime.
With $J = `r s1_3$J`$ there are `r 2^s1_3$J` patterns and
$N = `r format(s1_3$N, big.mark=",")`$ respondents, and
`r if (isTRUE(s1c$n_obs == s1c$n_cells)) paste0("every pattern is observed; the rarest appears ", s1c$min_count, " times") else paste0(s1c$n_obs, " of them are observed")`.
What the table shows instead is concentration: a few patterns carry much of the
mass.

For $J \leq 10$ items and $N$ in the thousands the full distribution is
enumerable. Below we tabulate every $2^J$ pattern and display the empirical
$p(\mathbf{x})$.

```{r}
#| label: fig-manifest-dist
#| fig-cap: !expr s1c$caption

patterns <- s1_3$patterns |>
  arrange(desc(count)) |>
  mutate(
    rank        = row_number(),
    p_obs       = count / s1_3$N,
    observed    = count > 0,
    pattern_str = apply(pick(all_of(s1_3$item_cols)), 1, paste, collapse = ""),
    tooltip     = paste0(
      "Pattern: ", pattern_str,
      "<br>p(x): ", signif(p_obs, 3),
      "<br>Count: ", count
    )
  )

n_observed   <- sum(patterns$observed)
n_unobserved <- sum(!patterns$observed)

p <- ggplot(patterns, aes(x = rank, y = p_obs, colour = observed, text = tooltip)) +
  geom_point(size = 1.2, alpha = 0.7) +
  scale_colour_manual(
    values = c("TRUE" = irw_blue, "FALSE" = irw_grey),
    labels = c("TRUE" = "Observed", "FALSE" = "Never seen"),
    name   = NULL
  ) +
  scale_y_log10(labels = scales::label_scientific()) +
  labs(
    x = "Pattern rank (most to least common)",
    y = "Empirical p(x)  [log scale]"
  )

plotly::ggplotly(p, tooltip = "text") |>
  plotly::layout(
    annotations = list(list(
      text      = paste0(n_observed, " of ", 2^s1_3$J,
                         " patterns observed; ", n_unobserved, " never appeared."),
      showarrow = FALSE,
      xref = "paper", yref = "paper",
      x = 0, y = -0.12,
      xanchor = "left", yanchor = "top",
      font = list(size = 11, color = "grey50")
    ))
  )
```

**What to notice.** `r if (isTRUE(s1c$n_obs == s1c$n_cells)) "Every pattern is there, but the" else "The"` mass is far from evenly
spread. The most common pattern`r if (isTRUE(s1c$top_is_all0[["obs"]])) " — all 0s —" else ""`
holds `r pct(s1c$top1[["obs"]])` of respondents, and the five most common hold
`r pct(s1c$top5[["obs"]])`. One summary of the spread is the entropy $H$ of
$p(\mathbf{x})$ in bits, or $2^H$, the number of equally likely patterns that
would have the same entropy: here `r round(s1c$eff[["obs"]], 1)` effective
patterns out of a possible `r s1c$n_cells`. The independence model of Section 2,
in which the items share nothing, is much flatter. Its most likely pattern gets `r pct(s1c$top1[["ind"]])`,
against `r pct(s1c$top1[["obs"]])` observed; it spreads the mass over `r round(s1c$eff[["ind"]], 1)` effective patterns, and
it puts `r round(s1c$all1_ratio)` times too little on the all-1s pattern. The
difference in entropy, $H_\text{ind} - H_\text{obs} =
`r round(s1c$multi, 2)`$ bits, is the information the items share. The rank-1
log-quadratic model of Section 2 recovers nearly all of it: top pattern
`r pct(s1c$top1[["rq"]])`, `r round(s1c$eff[["rq"]], 1)` effective patterns,
`r pct(s1c$rq_share)` of the entropy gap.

`r if (isTRUE(s1c$n_obs == s1c$n_cells)) "Sparsity, then, is not this table's problem. It becomes one" else "Sparsity is already visible here, and it gets worse"` as $J$ grows —
$2^J$ doubles with every item and $N$ does not — and that is why a
$2^J$-parameter saturated model is hopeless in general. The loglinear
parameterisation in Section 2 is the response.

The [bits-per-item vignette](bits_per_item.qmd#answer-patterns) uses this same
distribution to count how much a test tells you about a person.

### Concentration across the corpus

```{r}
#| label: s1-concentration-corpus
#| echo: false
#| eval: true

# The corpus version of the numbers above: one row per table, from
# vignettes/dutch_identity_gapshare.R with CONCENTRATION=1.
cc_path <- "dutchdata/concentration_tables.csv"
cc <- if (file.exists(cc_path)) read.csv(cc_path, stringsAsFactors = FALSE) else NULL
cq <- function(x, p = c(.25, .5, .75)) quantile(x, p, names = FALSE, na.rm = TRUE)
cc_sum <- if (!is.null(cc) && s1_3$table_name %in% cc$table) {
  this <- cc[cc$table == s1_3$table_name, ]
  big  <- cc$J >= 8
  list(
    n = nrow(cc), j_min = min(cc$J), j_max = max(cc$J),
    mi = cq(cc$multi_info_bits), cut = cq(cc$eff_reduction),
    rq = cq(cc$rq_share_of_multi), ratio = cq(cc$top1_ratio),
    this_mi = this$multi_info_bits, this_ratio = this$top1_ratio,
    this_mi_pctl = mean(cc$multi_info_bits < this$multi_info_bits),
    this_ratio_pctl = mean(cc$top1_ratio < this$top1_ratio),
    n_big = sum(big),
    frac_lo = min(cc$frac_observed[big]), frac_hi = max(cc$frac_observed[big]),
    mi_mm = median(cc$multi_info_bits_mm), mi_cs = median(cc$multi_info_bits_cs),
    rq_mm = median(cc$rq_share_of_multi_mm),
    mi_big = median(cc$multi_info_bits[big]), mi_big_mm = median(cc$multi_info_bits_mm[big]),
    mi_big_cs = median(cc$multi_info_bits_cs[big]),
    frac_med = median(cc$frac_observed[big]),
    cut_mm = median(cc$eff_reduction_mm), cut_cs = median(cc$eff_reduction_cs),
    rq_cs = median(cc$rq_share_of_multi_cs),
    rq_big = median(cc$rq_share_of_multi[big]), rq_big_cs = median(cc$rq_share_of_multi_cs[big]),
    shift_mm = median(cc$multi_info_bits - cc$multi_info_bits_mm),
    shift_cs = median(cc$multi_info_bits - cc$multi_info_bits_cs),
    shift_max_mm = max(cc$multi_info_bits - cc$multi_info_bits_mm),
    shift_max_cs = max(cc$multi_info_bits - cc$multi_info_bits_cs),
    top1_med = median(cc$top1_obs), top5_med = median(cc$top5_obs),
    effr_obs = median(cc$eff_obs / 2^cc$J), effr_ind = median(cc$eff_ind / 2^cc$J),
    n_all0 = sum(cc$top_pattern_obs == "all0"), n_all1 = sum(cc$top_pattern_obs == "all1"),
    n_ext_ind_miss = sum(cc$top_pattern_obs != "other" & cc$top_pattern_ind == "other"),
    n_ext_rq_miss  = sum(cc$top_pattern_obs != "other" & cc$top_pattern_rq == "other"),
    rho_j = cor(cc$J, cc$rq_share_of_multi, method = "spearman")
  )
} else list(n = NA, j_min = NA, j_max = NA, mi = rep(NA, 3), cut = rep(NA, 3),
            rq = rep(NA, 3), ratio = rep(NA, 3), this_mi = NA, this_ratio = NA,
            this_mi_pctl = NA, this_ratio_pctl = NA, n_big = NA, frac_lo = NA,
            frac_hi = NA, frac_med = NA, mi_mm = NA, mi_cs = NA, rq_mm = NA,
            mi_big = NA, mi_big_mm = NA, mi_big_cs = NA, cut_mm = NA, cut_cs = NA,
            rq_cs = NA, rq_big = NA, rq_big_cs = NA, shift_mm = NA, shift_cs = NA,
            shift_max_mm = NA, shift_max_cs = NA)
p0 <- function(x) sprintf("%.0f%%", 100 * x)
```

Is this concentration a quirk of one table? We compute the same summaries for
the `r cc_sum$n` IRW tables in the corpus sweep described in Section 2 (binary
items, $`r cc_sum$j_min` \le J \le `r cc_sum$j_max`$). Concentration is the
rule. In the median table the most common pattern holds
`r p0(cc_sum$top1_med)` of respondents and the five most common hold
`r p0(cc_sum$top5_med)`; the effective number of patterns, $2^H$, is
`r p0(cc_sum$effr_obs)` of the $2^J$ possible, against `r p0(cc_sum$effr_ind)`
under independence. Independence spreads the mass too thinly in every table
(@fig-concentration-corpus, left), as it must: the gap is the multi-information
$M = H_\text{ind} - H_\text{obs}$, which is never negative.

The extremes carry much of it. The most common pattern is all 0s in
`r cc_sum$n_all0` tables and all 1s in `r cc_sum$n_all1`. Independence misses
that in `r cc_sum$n_ext_ind_miss` of those
`r cc_sum$n_all0 + cc_sum$n_all1` tables, predicting a mixed pattern as the most
common; the rank-1 log-quadratic misses it in `r cc_sum$n_ext_rq_miss`.

```{r}
#| label: fig-concentration-corpus
#| fig-cap: "Pattern concentration across the corpus, one point per IRW table; the circled point is the table analysed in this vignette. Left: effective number of patterns 2^H as a share of the 2^J possible, under independence (horizontal) and observed (vertical); every table falls below the dashed line. Right: the multi-information M, the bits by which the observed distribution is more concentrated than independence predicts, against the part of M the rank-1 log-quadratic model reproduces, on log scales; points on the dashed line are fully reproduced."
#| fig-height: 4.2
#| fig-width: 9

cc_plot <- cc |>
  mutate(rq_bits = rq_share_of_multi * multi_info_bits,
         effr_obs = eff_obs / 2^J, effr_ind = eff_ind / 2^J,
         tooltip = paste0(
           "<b>", table, "</b>",
           "<br>J = ", J, ", N = ", format(N, big.mark = ","),
           "<br>Effective patterns: ", round(eff_obs, 1), " observed, ",
           round(eff_ind, 1), " independence (of ", 2^J, ")",
           "<br>Top pattern: ", sprintf("%.0f%%", 100 * top1_obs),
           " of respondents (", top_pattern_obs, ")",
           "<br>M = ", sprintf("%.3f", multi_info_bits), " bits; rank-1 reproduces ",
           sprintf("%.0f%%", 100 * rq_share_of_multi)))
cc_this <- cc_plot[cc_plot$table == s1_3$table_name, ]
j_col <- scale_colour_gradient(low = "#9ecae1", high = "#08306b", breaks = c(4, 6, 8, 10),
                               name = "Items (J)")
pa <- ggplot(cc_plot, aes(x = effr_ind, y = effr_obs, text = tooltip)) +
  geom_abline(slope = 1, intercept = 0, linetype = "dashed", colour = irw_grey) +
  geom_point(aes(colour = J), alpha = 0.75, size = 1.9) +
  geom_point(data = cc_this, shape = 21, size = 3.6, stroke = 1.1,
             colour = "grey15", fill = NA) +
  scale_x_continuous(labels = scales::percent, limits = c(0, 1)) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::percent, limits = c(0, 1)) +
  j_col +
  labs(x = "Effective patterns, independence", y = "Effective patterns, observed")
pb <- ggplot(cc_plot, aes(x = multi_info_bits, y = rq_bits, text = tooltip)) +
  geom_abline(slope = 1, intercept = 0, linetype = "dashed", colour = irw_grey) +
  geom_point(aes(colour = J), alpha = 0.75, size = 1.9) +
  geom_point(data = cc_this, shape = 21, size = 3.6, stroke = 1.1,
             colour = "grey15", fill = NA) +
  scale_x_log10() + scale_y_log10() + j_col +
  labs(x = "Multi-information M (bits)", y = "Reproduced by rank-1 model (bits)")
# hover works on both panels; the colour bar is shown once
pa_ly <- plotly::ggplotly(pa, tooltip = "text")
pb_ly <- plotly::ggplotly(pb, tooltip = "text") |> plotly::hide_colorbar()
plotly::subplot(pa_ly, pb_ly, nrows = 1, margin = 0.08, titleX = TRUE, titleY = TRUE) |>
  plotly::layout(annotations = list(list(
    text = "Hover over a point to see the table.", showarrow = FALSE,
    xref = "paper", yref = "paper", x = 0, y = -0.2,
    xanchor = "left", yanchor = "top", font = list(size = 11, color = "grey50"))))
```

In the median table the items share $M = `r sprintf("%.3f", cc_sum$mi[2])`$
bits (IQR `r sprintf("%.3f", cc_sum$mi[1])`–`r sprintf("%.3f", cc_sum$mi[3])`),
and since $2^{H_\text{obs}} / 2^{H_\text{ind}} = 2^{-M}$ that is a cut of about
`r p0(cc_sum$cut[2])` in the effective number of patterns. Across tables $M$
runs from `r sprintf("%.2f", min(cc$multi_info_bits))` to
`r sprintf("%.1f", max(cc$multi_info_bits))` bits, and the rank-1 model tracks
it over that whole range, reproducing a median `r p0(cc_sum$rq[2])` of it
(@fig-concentration-corpus, right). What it misses grows with the number of
items (Spearman $\rho = `r sprintf("%.2f", cc_sum$rho_j)`$ between $J$ and the
reproduced share), a pattern Section 2 returns to. This vignette's table is
concentrated but not an outlier: its $M$ of
`r sprintf("%.2f", cc_sum$this_mi)` bits exceeds `r p0(cc_sum$this_mi_pctl)` of
tables, and its most common pattern is `r sprintf("%.1f", cc_sum$this_ratio)`
times as frequent as independence predicts, against
`r sprintf("%.2f", cc_sum$ratio[2])` in the median table.

These are plug-in entropies, which are biased downward when cells are sparse —
most at $J \ge 8$, where a median of only `r p0(cc_sum$frac_med)` of the $2^J$
patterns are observed. Bias-corrected estimates (Miller–Madow, Chao–Shen) move
single tables by a median
`r sprintf("%.3f", min(cc_sum$shift_mm, cc_sum$shift_cs))`–`r sprintf("%.3f", max(cc_sum$shift_mm, cc_sum$shift_cs))`
bits and, if anything, raise the rank-1 share (at $J \ge 8$ from
`r p0(cc_sum$rq_big)` to `r p0(cc_sum$rq_big_cs)` with Chao–Shen). The full
breakdown is in `vignettes/dutchdata/concentration_summary.md`.

---

## Section 2: Three loglinear models

The rest of the page fits three nested models to the $2^J$ pattern counts. Each
is a Poisson regression of the counts on functions of the item responses; they
differ only in how much association among items they allow.

Under **independence** — no latent variable, no associations — $\log
p(\mathbf{x})$ is linear in the item responses,

$$\log p(\mathbf{x}) = \alpha + \sum_{j=1}^{J} \beta_j x_j ,$$

with $J + 1$ parameters. Section 1 has already shown what this misses: it
spreads the mass too thinly and badly underpredicts the patterns where most
items are answered the same way.

The **second-order exponential (SOE)** model adds every pairwise interaction,

$$\log p(\mathbf{x}) = \alpha + \sum_j \beta_j x_j + \sum_{j < k} \gamma_{jk}\, x_j x_k ,$$

for $1 + J + \binom{J}{2}$ parameters. The $J \times J$ matrix
$\boldsymbol{\Gamma}$ (with $\Gamma_{jk} = \gamma_{jk}$ and $\Gamma_{jj} = 0$)
holds all pairwise associations after removing main effects.

Holland's log-quadratic approximation [@holland1990dutch] predicts that
$\boldsymbol{\Gamma}$ is *approximately rank-1*, $\Gamma_{jk} \approx \gamma_j
\gamma_k$, so that the interactions collapse to

$$\log p(\mathbf{x}) \approx \alpha + \sum_j \beta_j' x_j + \frac{1}{2}\!\left(\sum_j \gamma_j x_j\right)^{\!2},$$

the **restricted log-quadratic** model, with $1 + 2J$ parameters.

### Model comparison

```{r}
#| label: tbl-bic
#| tbl-cap: "Log-likelihood and BIC for three nested loglinear models, all fitted by Poisson maximum likelihood to the same table of 2^J pattern counts with zero cells included. The restricted log-quadratic uses 2J + 1 parameters; the full SOE uses 1 + J + J(J-1)/2. BIC uses n = N respondents for every row."

s1_3$bic_table |>
  mutate(
    across(c(Log_lik, BIC), \(x) round(x, 1)),
    BIC_delta = round(BIC - min(BIC), 1)
  ) |>
  rename(`ΔBIC vs. best` = BIC_delta, `Log-lik` = Log_lik) |>
  knitr::kable(align = "lrrr")
```

The models are nested — independence is the log-quadratic with $\gamma = 0$,
and the log-quadratic is the SOE with $\Gamma_{jk}$ forced to
$\gamma_j \gamma_k$ — so the log-likelihoods must increase down the table, and
they do.[^fitting]

[^fitting]: All three are fitted by Poisson maximum likelihood to the same
$2^J$ counts, zero cells included, so the log-likelihoods share one scale; each
has a free intercept, so the multinomial log-likelihoods differ from the Poisson
ones by the same constant
(`r paste(sprintf("%.1f", s1_3$ll_multinomial), collapse = ", ")`). The rank-1
model is fitted directly rather than as a GLM, since $\gamma$ enters only
through $(\mathbf{x}'\gamma)^2$ and is identified only up to sign; of
`r s1_3$rq_convergence$n_starts` starting values,
`r s1_3$rq_convergence$n_at_best` reached the reported optimum.

The key question is whether the restricted log-quadratic — which enforces rank-1
structure on $\boldsymbol{\Gamma}$ — captures most of the association signal
while using only $1 + 2J$ parameters instead of $1 + J + \binom{J}{2}$. It
captures nearly all of it: the rank-1 model recovers
**`r sprintf("%.1f%%", 100 * s1_3$rq_gap_share)`** of the
independence-to-SOE log-likelihood gap,
$(\ell_{\text{rq}} - \ell_{\text{ind}})/(\ell_{\text{soe}} - \ell_{\text{ind}})$,
with `r s1_3$bic_table$Parameters[3] - s1_3$bic_table$Parameters[2]` fewer
parameters. BIC still prefers the full SOE, but only by
`r sprintf("%.1f", round(s1_3$bic_table$BIC[2], 1) - round(s1_3$bic_table$BIC[3], 1))`
— small beside the
`r sprintf("%.1f", round(s1_3$bic_table$BIC[1], 1) - round(s1_3$bic_table$BIC[3], 1))`
that separates independence from the SOE.

```{r}
#| label: fig-model-fit
#| fig-cap: "Observed vs. fitted log-probability for each of the three loglinear models across all observed response patterns. Points on the dashed diagonal indicate perfect fit; scatter above the diagonal means the model over-predicts that pattern."
#| fig-height: 3.5

fit_df <- s1_3$patterns |>
  filter(!is.na(log_p_obs)) |>
  select(log_p_obs, log_p_ind, log_p_rq, log_p_soe) |>
  pivot_longer(
    cols      = c(log_p_ind, log_p_rq, log_p_soe),
    names_to  = "model",
    values_to = "log_p_fit"
  ) |>
  filter(!is.na(log_p_fit)) |>
  mutate(model = factor(recode(model,
    log_p_ind = "Independence",
    log_p_rq  = "Log-quadratic\n(rank-1 Γ)",
    log_p_soe = "Full SOE"
  ), levels = c("Independence", "Log-quadratic\n(rank-1 Γ)", "Full SOE")))

ggplot(fit_df, aes(x = log_p_obs, y = log_p_fit)) +
  geom_abline(slope = 1, intercept = 0, linetype = "dashed", colour = irw_grey) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.6, size = 1.5, colour = irw_blue) +
  facet_wrap(~ model, nrow = 1) +
  labs(
    x       = "Observed log-probability",
    y       = "Fitted log-probability",
    caption = paste0(
      nrow(s1_3$patterns |> filter(!is.na(log_p_obs))),
      " observed response patterns from ", s1_3$table_name, "."
    )
  )
```

### Is Γ rank-1?

The approximation's prediction about $\boldsymbol{\Gamma}$ concerns the
off-diagonal entries only. Since $x_j^2 = x_j$ for binary items,

$$\frac{1}{2}\!\left(\sum_j \gamma_j x_j\right)^{\!2}
  = \frac{1}{2}\sum_j \gamma_j^2 x_j \;+\; \sum_{j<k} \gamma_j \gamma_k x_j x_k,$$

so the squared terms are absorbed into the main effects and the prediction is
$\Gamma_{jk} \approx \gamma_j \gamma_k$ for $j \neq k$. @fig-gamma-rank1-scatter
plots one against the other. To summarise it in a number, we fit the best rank-1
structure to the off-diagonals, weighting each entry by $1/\mathrm{SE}^2$ from
the SOE fit, and ask what share of the weighted sum of squares it explains.

```{r}
#| label: fig-gamma-rank1-scatter
#| fig-cap: "Off-diagonal entries of Γ from the full SOE fit against γⱼγₖ from the fitted restricted log-quadratic model, with the 45° line. Error bars are ±1 SE of the SOE coefficient."
#| fig-height: 3.8

sc <- s1_3$gamma_rank1$scatter

ggplot(sc, aes(x = gamma_pred, y = gamma_soe)) +
  geom_abline(slope = 1, intercept = 0, colour = irw_grey, linetype = "dashed") +
  geom_errorbar(aes(ymin = gamma_soe - se, ymax = gamma_soe + se),
                width = 0, colour = irw_grey, alpha = 0.8) +
  geom_point(colour = irw_blue, size = 2.4, alpha = 0.9) +
  labs(x = expression(gamma[j] * gamma[k] ~ "(restricted log-quadratic)"),
       y = expression(Gamma[jk] ~ "(full SOE)"))
```

```{r}
#| label: s3-2pl-baseline
#| echo: false
#| eval: true

# Reference distribution: a unidimensional 2PL, from vignettes/dutch_identity_2pl_baseline.R
b2_path <- "dutchdata/dutch_identity_2pl_baseline.rds"
b2 <- if (file.exists(b2_path)) readRDS(b2_path) else
  list(n_sim = NA, n_failed = 0, population_share = NA, observed_share = NA,
       sim_summary = list(median = NA, lo = NA, hi = NA, min = NA),
       n_below_observed = NA, sim_share = numeric(),
       ll_2pl = NA, ll_multinomial = c(ind = NA, rq = NA, soe = NA))
b2_n <- length(b2$sim_share)
b2_all_above <- isTRUE(b2$n_below_observed == 0)
p1 <- function(x) sprintf("%.1f%%", 100 * x)
```

A share on its own proves little, since a short test at finite $N$ will never
return an exactly rank-1 $\boldsymbol{\Gamma}$. So we need a reference: what
share does a unidimensional model produce at this $J$ and $N$? We fit a 2PL
with normal $\theta$ to this table, simulate `r b2_n` tables of counts from it,
refit the SOE to each, and recompute the share. The replicates have median
`r p1(b2$sim_summary$median)`, with 95% in
[`r p1(b2$sim_summary$lo)`, `r p1(b2$sim_summary$hi)`]. (Simulating from the
fitted log-quadratic model instead gives nearly the same band.) The observed
share is `r p1(s1_3$gamma_rank1$rank1_weighted$share)`, below
`r if (b2_all_above) paste0("every one of the ", b2_n) else paste0(b2_n - b2$n_below_observed, " of the ", b2_n)`
replicates.
`r if (b2_all_above) "So the off-diagonals of $\\boldsymbol{\\Gamma}$ are **not** rank-1, and the departure is not one the fitted 2PL reproduces. That is weaker than saying no unidimensional model could produce it; we have checked one." else "A unidimensional 2PL at this $J$ and $N$ can produce a share this low, so the departure is not by itself evidence against unidimensionality."`
In the scatter, `r s1_3$gamma_rank1$n_resid_z_gt_3` of the
`r s1_3$gamma_rank1$n_offdiag` pairs sit more than three standard errors off the
line, the largest being
`r s1_3$gamma_rank1$worst_resid$item1`–`r s1_3$gamma_rank1$worst_resid$item2`
at `r sprintf("%.1f", s1_3$gamma_rank1$worst_resid$z)` SE, which looks like
local dependence between particular item pairs.

The two findings are not in conflict. Rank-1 is rejected as a description of
$\boldsymbol{\Gamma}$ while remaining an excellent *predictive* approximation:
the extra interaction parameters the SOE spends on the non-rank-1 structure buy
it only `r sprintf("%.1f%%", 100 * (1 - s1_3$rq_gap_share))` of the likelihood
gap. Statistical rejection and practical adequacy answer different questions,
and at $N = `r format(s1_3$N, big.mark=",")`$ a real but small departure is
detectable without being important for prediction.

### Is the economy unusual?

Everything above concerns one instrument. The economy claim — that the restricted log-quadratic model closes almost all
of the gap between independence and the full SOE —
is worth asking of the corpus, because on one table it could be a property of
these five items rather than of item response data.

So we ask it of every IRW table that admits the same three fits: binary items,
$`r gs_sum$j_min` \le J \le `r gs_sum$j_max`$, and enough respondents to
populate $2^J$ cells — `r gs_sum$n_tables` tables. We compute the same ratio
out of sample, by five-fold cross-validation over respondents, because in sample
it is inflated when $J$ is small. Out of sample it is not bounded by 1, so a few
tables land slightly above it.

Fitted cell probabilities are floored at $1/(10 N_{\text{train}})$ before
scoring, so that one held-out respondent in a numerically empty cell cannot
dominate a fold. Flooring regularises the predictions; what justifies it is
that it barely matters in aggregate (the median is
`r sprintf("%.3f", gs_sum$med_out_raw)` unfloored,
`r sprintf("%.3f", gs_sum$med_out)` floored), though it moves
`r gs_sum$n_floor_moves` of the `r gs_sum$n_usable` tables by more than 0.05, at
most `r sprintf("%.2f", gs_sum$max_floor_move)`. Both versions are in the CSV.

```{r}
#| label: fig-gapshare-corpus
#| fig-cap: "Held-out gap share for every IRW table admitting the three fits, against the number of items. Each blue point is one table. The dashed line is the median over all tables — the 96.3% quoted below. Red segments are per-J medians, which is where the decline with J shows up. The circled point is the table analysed in this vignette. A value of 1 means the restricted log-quadratic model captures all of the held-out predictive gain the full SOE makes over independence."
#| fig-height: 4.2

gs_u    <- gs[gs$share_out_usable, ]
gs_this <- gs_u[gs_u$table == s1_3$table_name, ]
set.seed(1)   # fixed jitter, so the figure is stable across renders
gs_u$xj <- gs_u$J + runif(nrow(gs_u), -0.14, 0.14)
gs_u$tooltip <- paste0(
  "<b>", gs_u$table, "</b>",
  "<br>J = ", gs_u$J, ", N = ", format(gs_u$N, big.mark = ","),
  "<br>Held-out gap share: ", sprintf("%.3f", gs_u$share_out_floor),
  " (in sample ", sprintf("%.3f", gs_u$share_in), ")",
  "<br>Gain over independence, nats per respondent: ",
  sprintf("%.3f", gs_u$cv_gap_rq_nats), " rank-1, ",
  sprintf("%.3f", gs_u$cv_gap_soe_nats), " SOE",
  ifelse(is.na(gs_u$construct_type) | gs_u$construct_type == "", "",
         paste0("<br>", gs_u$construct_type)))

p5 <- ggplot(gs_u, aes(x = xj, y = share_out_floor)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = gs_sum$med_out, linetype = "dashed",
             colour = irw_grey) +
  annotate("text", x = gs_sum$j_max + 0.42, y = gs_sum$med_out,
           label = sprintf("median %.3f", gs_sum$med_out),
           hjust = 1, vjust = -0.6, size = 3.2, colour = irw_grey) +
  geom_point(aes(text = tooltip), alpha = 0.5, colour = irw_blue, size = 1.9) +
  geom_segment(data = gs_sum$by_j,
               aes(x = J - 0.32, xend = J + 0.32,
                   y = share_out_floor, yend = share_out_floor),
               colour = irw_red, linewidth = 1) +
  geom_point(data = gs_this, aes(x = J, y = share_out_floor),
             shape = 21, size = 3.6, stroke = 1.1,
             colour = "grey15", fill = NA) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = gs_sum$j_min:gs_sum$j_max,
                     limits = c(gs_sum$j_min - 0.45, gs_sum$j_max + 0.45)) +
  labs(x = "Number of items (J)", y = "Held-out gap share")
plotly::ggplotly(p5, tooltip = "text") |>
  plotly::layout(annotations = list(list(
    text = paste0("Dashed: median over all ", gs_sum$n_usable,
                  " tables. Red: per-J medians. Circled: ", s1_3$table_name,
                  ". Hover over a point to see the table."),
    showarrow = FALSE, xref = "paper", yref = "paper", x = 0, y = -0.2,
    xanchor = "left", yanchor = "top", font = list(size = 11, color = "grey50"))))
```

**What to notice.** The dashed line is the headline: in the median table the
restricted log-quadratic model captures `r sprintf("%.1f%%", 100 * gs_sum$med_out)`
of the held-out gain the SOE makes over independence (IQR
[`r sprintf("%.2f", gs_sum$q1_out)`, `r sprintf("%.2f", gs_sum$q3_out)`]). The
circled point is this vignette's table, at
`r sprintf("%.1f%%", 100 * gs_sum$this_out)` — above the median but well inside
the cloud of its $J = `r s1_3$J`$ neighbours, so ordinary rather than
exceptional. In absolute terms the residual is small too: across tables the
restricted model is worth a median
`r sprintf("%.3f", gs_sum$med_rq_nats)` nats per held-out respondent over
independence, the full SOE `r sprintf("%.3f", gs_sum$med_soe_nats)`, and the
median table's own difference between the two is
`r sprintf("%.4f", gs_sum$med_beyond_nats)` nats — about
`r sprintf("%.0f%%", 100 * gs_sum$med_beyond_nats / gs_sum$med_rq_nats)` of what
the restricted model buys. The economy claim is a property of these data broadly,
not of this instrument.

It does decay with $J$, monotonically over most of the range, from
`r sprintf("%.2f", gs_sum$by_j$share_out_floor[1])` at $J = `r gs_sum$by_j$J[1]`$
to
`r sprintf("%.2f", tail(gs_sum$by_j$share_out_floor, 1))` at
$J = `r tail(gs_sum$by_j$J, 1)`$. Whether that is about item count or about what
long instruments measure, these data cannot say: more items means more pairs
that *can* depart from rank-1, and it also means instruments that sprawl across
facets. The low outliers favour the second reading — the worst cases are item
sets that were never indicators of one trait, such as a battery asking which
*sources* someone used for COVID information, or a short subscale that mixes
material deprivation with supervision. There the departure from rank-1 says more
about how the items were assembled than about the model.

Two cautions. The ratio's denominator can be small: for `r gs_sum$n_thin` of the
`r gs_sum$n_usable` tables the full SOE beats independence by under 0.05 nats
per respondent, and a low share there means there was little to explain rather
than that the restricted model failed. More importantly, this is a share of
*second-order* association. The SOE is itself a restricted model — no three-way
or higher interactions — so a table at 96% has the restricted model capturing 96% of
what the pairwise model captures, which is silent about dependence neither model
can see. The per-table numbers, the exclusions and the diagnostics are in
`vignettes/dutchdata/gapshare_summary.md`.

### Rejected, but adequate?

```{r}
#| label: s2-rank1-corpus
#| echo: false
#| eval: true

# The rank-1 test of "Is Γ rank-1?", run on every table by
# vignettes/dutch_identity_gapshare.R with RANK1=1.
r1_path <- "dutchdata/rank1_tables.csv"
r1 <- if (file.exists(r1_path)) read.csv(r1_path, stringsAsFactors = FALSE) else NULL
r1_sum <- if (!is.null(r1)) {
  r1$short <- r1$sim_median - r1$share_obs
  r1$rej   <- r1$p_emp < 0.05
  r1$boundary <- r1$max_slope > 10   # a slope still climbing at the cycle cap
  u <- r1[r1$share_out_usable, ]
  nq <- cut(r1$N, quantile(r1$N, 0:4 / 4), include.lowest = TRUE)
  list(
    n = nrow(r1), n_sim = median(r1$n_sim + r1$n_sim_failed),
    n_rej = sum(r1$rej), frac_rej = mean(r1$rej),
    n_all_below = sum(r1$n_below == 0),
    n_boundary = sum(r1$boundary), n_rej_boundary = sum(r1$rej & r1$boundary),
    frac_rej_nb = mean(r1$rej[!r1$boundary]),
    rej_by_j = tapply(r1$rej, r1$J, mean),
    rej_nq = tapply(r1$rej, nq, mean),
    short_med = median(r1$short), short_q = quantile(r1$short, c(.25, .75), names = FALSE),
    rho_short_gap = cor(u$short, u$share_out_floor, method = "spearman"),
    rho_short_n = cor(r1$short, log(r1$N), method = "spearman"),
    n_u = nrow(u), n_rej_u = sum(u$rej),
    n_rej_hi = sum(u$rej & u$share_out_floor >= 0.9),
    gap_rej = median(u$share_out_floor[u$rej]),
    gap_acc = median(u$share_out_floor[!u$rej]),
    n_lo = sum(u$short < 0.1), gap_lo = median(u$share_out_floor[u$short < 0.1]),
    n_hi = sum(u$short >= 0.1), gap_hi = median(u$share_out_floor[u$short >= 0.1]),
    gap_hi_p10 = quantile(u$share_out_floor[u$short >= 0.1], 0.1, names = FALSE),
    this = r1[r1$table == s1_3$table_name, ]
  )
} else NULL
```

The single-table result — rank-1 rejected, but cheap to ignore for prediction —
might be a feature of this table. So we run the same test on all
`r r1_sum$n` tables: fit a 2PL with normal $\theta$ to each, simulate
`r r1_sum$n_sim` tables of counts from it at the observed $N$, refit the SOE to
each, and ask where the observed weighted rank-1 share falls.

Rank-1 is rejected ($p < 0.05$) for `r r1_sum$n_rej` of the `r r1_sum$n`
tables, and for `r r1_sum$n_all_below` the observed share is below every
replicate. That is not simply a matter of sample size. The rejection rate does
rise with $N$ — from `r p0(r1_sum$rej_nq[1])` in the smallest quarter of tables to
`r p0(r1_sum$rej_nq[4])` in the largest — and it also rises with $J$,
from `r p0(r1_sum$rej_by_j[["4"]])` at $J = 4$ to every table from
$J = `r min(as.integer(names(r1_sum$rej_by_j))[r1_sum$rej_by_j == 1])`$ up. And the
*size* of the departure, the gap between the 2PL replicates' median share and the
observed one, is nearly unrelated to $N$ (Spearman $\rho =
`r sprintf("%.2f", r1_sum$rho_short_n)`$ with $\log N$). The departures are
real and common.

```{r}
#| label: fig-rank1-corpus
#| fig-cap: "Departure from rank-1 against predictive economy, one point per IRW table. Horizontal axis: how far the observed weighted rank-1 share of Γ falls below the median of replicates simulated from the table's own fitted 2PL (log scale; tables at or above the 2PL median are drawn at the left edge). Vertical axis: the held-out gap share from the previous figure. Filled points reject rank-1 at p < 0.05. The circled point is the table analysed in this vignette."
#| fig-height: 4.2

r1_plot <- r1[r1$share_out_usable, ]
r1_plot$short_plot <- pmax(r1_plot$short, 1e-3)
r1_plot$tooltip <- paste0(
  "<b>", r1_plot$table, "</b>",
  "<br>J = ", r1_plot$J, ", N = ", format(r1_plot$N, big.mark = ","),
  "<br>Rank-1 share: ", sprintf("%.3f", r1_plot$share_obs), " observed; 2PL replicates ",
  sprintf("%.3f", r1_plot$sim_median), " [", sprintf("%.3f", r1_plot$sim_lo), ", ",
  sprintf("%.3f", r1_plot$sim_hi), "]",
  "<br>p = ", sprintf("%.3f", r1_plot$p_emp),
  ifelse(r1_plot$rej, " (rank-1 rejected)", " (not rejected)"),
  "<br>Held-out gap share: ", sprintf("%.3f", r1_plot$share_out_floor),
  ifelse(r1_plot$boundary, "<br>2PL slope still climbing (boundary fit)", ""))
p6 <- ggplot(r1_plot, aes(x = short_plot, y = share_out_floor)) +
  geom_point(aes(shape = rej, text = tooltip), colour = irw_blue, size = 2.1, alpha = 0.8) +
  geom_point(data = r1_plot[r1_plot$table == s1_3$table_name, ],
             shape = 21, size = 3.8, stroke = 1.1, colour = "grey15", fill = NA) +
  scale_shape_manual(values = c(`TRUE` = 16, `FALSE` = 1),
                     labels = c(`TRUE` = "rank-1 rejected", `FALSE` = "not rejected"),
                     name = NULL) +
  scale_x_log10() +
  labs(x = "Shortfall of rank-1 share below the 2PL reference",
       y = "Held-out gap share") +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom")
plotly::ggplotly(p6, tooltip = "text") |>
  plotly::layout(legend = list(orientation = "h", x = 0, y = -0.25))
```

The figure puts the two findings side by side. That they move together is no
surprise — both measure the same non-rank-1 structure in the SOE, once through
$\boldsymbol{\Gamma}$ and once through likelihood
(Spearman $\rho = `r sprintf("%.2f", r1_sum$rho_short_gap)`$). What is
informative is the shape. For the `r r1_sum$n_lo` tables whose shortfall is
under 0.1, the median gap share is `r p1(r1_sum$gap_lo)`. For the
`r r1_sum$n_hi` beyond it the median is still `r p1(r1_sum$gap_hi)`, but the
lower tail is long: a tenth of them fall below `r p0(r1_sum$gap_hi_p10)`. Small
departures cost almost nothing, and the expensive cases are the large ones. Most rejections are cheap: of the `r r1_sum$n_rej_u` rejected tables,
`r r1_sum$n_rej_hi` still capture at least 90% of the SOE's
predictive gain (median `r p0(r1_sum$gap_rej)`, against
`r p0(r1_sum$gap_acc)` for tables where rank-1 survives). This vignette's table
is one of that majority.

One caveat about the reference. For `r r1_sum$n_boundary` tables one 2PL
slope is still climbing when the fit stops (above 10, against at most
`r sprintf("%.1f", max(r1$max_slope[!r1$boundary]))` everywhere else) — an item
close to deterministic given the trait — so the reference there is a 2PL at the
edge of its parameter space. Excluding those tables, rank-1 is rejected for
`r p0(r1_sum$frac_rej_nb)` of the rest. Per-table results are in
`vignettes/dutchdata/rank1_tables.csv`.

---

## Where this leaves us

Across the `r gs_sum$n_usable` tables, two things are true. First, Holland's
log-quadratic form is economical: with $1 + 2J$ parameters, against
$1 + J + J(J-1)/2$ for the full pairwise model (16 against 56 at $J = 10$), it
captures a median `r sprintf("%.1f%%", 100 * gs_sum$med_out)` of what the
pairwise model gains over independence, out of sample. Second, it is usually
detectably imperfect: in `r r1_sum$n_rej` of the `r r1_sum$n` tables the item
associations depart from rank-1 by more than the table's own fitted 2PL would
produce. These do not conflict. Most departures are small and cost little in
prediction; a few are large and cost a lot. If the goal is predicting response
patterns, the approximation is good enough for most tables. If the goal is
finding item pairs that share something beyond the common trait, the departures
are where to look.

This is not to say that IRT guarantees the economy. The log-quadratic form is a
conjecture with known counterexamples [@zhang1997holland], so these are
findings about item response data as collected rather than consequences of the
theory. Holland also argues that a $D$-dimensional model leaves the
off-diagonals of $\boldsymbol{\Gamma}$ approximately rank $D$; testing that
for $D > 1$ would need a minimum-rank fit and a reference distribution at each
candidate rank, which we do not attempt here.

---

::: {.callout-warning}
## Limitations

**Pattern sparsity.** Sections 1–2 require $J \leq 10$ for pattern enumeration
to be feasible. The SOE loglinear approach does not generalise to large $J$.
:::

## Reproducibility

{{< include ../components/_source-links.qmd >}}

{{< include ../components/_data-version.qmd >}}

Results were computed on `r format(date_run, "%B %d, %Y")` with
`irw` version `r irw_pkg_version`. To regenerate:

```r
# 1. Re-run the compute script (from the project root)
source("vignettes/dutch_identity_compute.R")

# 2. Re-render this page
quarto::quarto_render("vignettes/dutch_identity.qmd")
```

The model-fitting and Γ-diagnostic helpers live in
`vignettes/dutch_identity_helpers.R`, which `dutch_identity_compute.R` sources.
`vignettes/dutch_identity_gamma_rerun.R` updates only the Section 2 Γ
diagnostics in the cached result, refitting the loglinear models from the stored
pattern counts and asserting that Table 1 is unchanged, so a figure fix does not
require re-running the corpus-wide sections.

The corpus sweep behind @fig-gapshare-corpus is a separate, slower job:
`vignettes/dutch_identity_gapshare.R` fits the three models to every eligible
IRW table and writes one row per table to
`vignettes/dutchdata/gapshare_tables.csv`, which is what this page reads.
`vignettes/dutch_identity_gapshare_report.R` turns that CSV into
`gapshare_summary.md` with the full breakdown, the exclusion counts and the
diagnosed outliers. Both pin the IRW version they ran against and cache per
table, so the sweep resumes rather than restarting.

The same script with `CONCENTRATION=1` writes the pattern-concentration
statistics behind @fig-concentration-corpus
(`vignettes/dutchdata/concentration_tables.csv`), and with `RANK1=1` runs the
rank-1 test against each table's fitted 2PL behind @fig-rank1-corpus
(`vignettes/dutchdata/rank1_tables.csv`). Both re-read exactly the tables in
`gapshare_tables.csv` at the IRW version that sweep used, and stop if the data
differ. The single-table 2PL reference in "Is Γ rank-1?" comes from
`vignettes/dutch_identity_2pl_baseline.R`.

::: {.callout-tip}
To cite the IRW datasets used, run:

```r
for (tbl in unique(s1_3$table_name)) {
  irw_save_bibtex(tbl, output_file = "vignettes/dutchdata/irw_references.bib",
                  append = TRUE)
}
```
:::
